title: Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models
one_liner: Measure when a group of language-model agents becomes a coordinated system instead of a set of isolated responders.
lead: A multi-agent language-model setup can look coordinated even when each agent is simply reacting to the same recent history. That makes evaluation hard, because apparent order may come from timing alone rather than real division of labor. This paper builds a data-driven test for higher-order coordination and uses it to show that prompt design can move a group from loose aggregates toward coordinated teams with differentiated roles and shared goals.

problem.h2: Why multi-agent success is hard to interpret
paras: When several agents produce answers over time, better group performance does not automatically mean that the group has become a real collective, because the agents may simply share the same external signal, repeat similar patterns, or benefit from luck in turn order. If that is the case, adding more agents gives the appearance of teamwork without the substance.

The hard question is whether the joint behavior contains information that cannot be assigned to any single agent alone. That is what the paper calls higher-order structure. A useful measure must separate genuine cross-agent complementarity from trivial coupling due to shared history or repeated exposure to the same task.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Measure how much predictive information exists only in the joint state of several agents across time, then compare prompt conditions to see when role differentiation and goal alignment create real coordination.

panels.title: 1. Same task, many agents
panels.viz_args: Three agents guess in turns with only group-level feedback
panels.caption: The setup withholds direct messaging, so any coordination must arise indirectly.

panels.title: 2. Surface order is not enough
panels.caption: Repeated structure can come from timing and shared signals, not from real teamwork.

panels.title: 3. Measure joint predictive information
panels.viz_args: Past group state -> future group state; separate shared, unique, and joint-only parts
panels.caption: The analysis asks what the group knows together that no single member carries alone.

panels.title: 4. Change the prompts
panels.viz_args: Control / personas / personas + think about others
panels.caption: Prompt changes create different group structures, which the measure can localize and compare.

panels.title: 5. Coordination appears in the joint term
panels.caption: A stronger joint-only term signals real complementarity because the group prediction needs multiple agents together.

steps.text: Collect time series from several agents solving the same task with only minimal group feedback, so that the analysis uses observed behavior instead of hand-written labels.
Measure how much the earlier states of agents tell you about later states, because coordination should leave a predictive trace across time.
Separate what is redundant, what belongs to one agent alone, and what exists only in the joint state, so that trivial coupling does not get mistaken for teamwork.
Run control, persona, and perspective-taking prompts, because the paper wants to test whether prompt design changes group structure rather than only final score.
Check whether strong joint-only information appears when the group solves the task better, so that the measure tracks productive coordination instead of empty synchrony.

paras: The paper changes how multi-agent systems are evaluated. Instead of asking only whether the final answers improve, it measures how the group state is organized across time and whether that organization depends on several agents acting together, because dependence on several agents is the signature of higher-order coordination rather than isolated success.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: joint-only predictive information
hidden.name: Cross-agent joint-only information over time
paras: The central hidden quantity is the part of future predictability that appears only when several agents are considered together. If one agent alone carries the same signal, that is not a joint-only effect. If the same signal is duplicated across all agents, that is redundancy. The joint-only part is the leftover signal that needs the combination.

This quantity matters because genuine coordination should create complementary behavior. One agent may explore, another may stabilize the group's guess, and a third may react to group errors. The future group state is then predictable from their combination in a way that no single agent can provide alone.

heat.caption: The darker joint-only cells are what the paper seeks. Those cells mark information that exists only in the combined state of several agents.

reads.html: Joint-only information is the part of group behavior you can predict only after looking at multiple agents together.
The method uses partial information decomposition of time-delayed mutual information to isolate redundancy, uniqueness, and the joint-only contribution in multi-agent dynamics.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: separate mere coupling from productive complementarity
paras: The method works because it analyzes dependence structure, not just outcome quality. Shared feedback can make all agents move in similar ways, but that only creates redundant information. Stronger final accuracy can also come from one unusually good agent, but that only raises a unique contribution. By decomposing the predictive signal, the analysis reveals whether the group has built a genuine combination effect that needs several agents at once.

Prompt design changes that structure. Personas can create stable differentiation because each agent keeps a distinct behavioral tendency across rounds. Adding an instruction to consider what others may do can create complementarity because each agent updates with the broader group in mind. When both appear together, the group can align on a common objective while still splitting responsibilities.

stages.s: Decompose into shared, unique, and joint-only parts
Evidence for aggregate behavior or coordinated collective

math.words: Start with the information that the past group state gives about the future group state. Then divide that total into pieces: repeated information, single-agent information, and the extra part that appears only when agents are combined.
symbols: time-delayed mutual information between the earlier and later group states
predictive information carried by one agent alone
the paper's name for predictive information that appears only in the joint state of several agents

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose three agents play repeated rounds of a guessing game.
Agent A tends to explore, agent B tends to stabilize the group's running best guess, and agent C reacts when the group misses in a particular direction.
Looking at A alone or B alone does not predict the next group move very well.
Looking at A and B together predicts more, because exploration and stabilization interact.
Adding C predicts even more when misses trigger a compensating move.
That extra predictive part is joint-only because it belongs to the combination, not to any one agent.

math.note: The decomposition matters because raw dependence can be inflated by shared timing, while the joint-only term isolates coordination that needs several agents together.

charts.title: Control prompt only
charts.note: Agents respond to the same task and feedback, but little structured complementarity appears because they lack stable roles and perspective-taking instructions.

charts.title: Personas + think about others
charts.note: The combined prompt raises coordination because agents keep distinct tendencies while adjusting to the expected behavior of teammates.

items.html: If all agents simply react to the same recent signal, the system may look organized even though no true coordination exists. The decomposition is needed because raw dependence alone cannot separate these cases.

items.b: Role prompts can create style without usefulness.
items.html: Personas may differentiate language patterns without helping task performance, so a role signal should be read together with the joint-only coordination term and outcome quality.

items.b: Small samples can distort the estimates.
items.html: Information estimates can drift when the number of rounds is low, because the decomposition needs enough observed transitions to stabilize.

items.b: Done right: coordinated groups balance alignment and specialization.
items.html: The strongest condition works because agents share the task goal while keeping complementary roles, so the group gains both consistency and division of labor.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a repeated group guessing task with three language-model agents and only a shared score after each round. Run three prompt settings: plain control, fixed personas, and fixed personas plus an instruction to consider what other agents may do. Record each agent's action at every round. Then compute a simple past-to-future dependence measure and a decomposition into shared, unique, and joint-only parts. The demo should show that stronger group performance lines up with a larger joint-only term, because productive coordination requires multiple agents to contribute complementary information.
demo.closing: The demo must show that prompt design can change the internal organization of a group, not only its final score.
